lessons.title: Volatility Strategies Across Regimes: Options Selling vs Options Buying

body.text: Options selling bets that realized volatility undershoots what the market priced in. Options buying bets it overshoots. This is the volatility dimension's own version of momentum versus mean reversion, and it deserves the same regime-conditional treatment.

children.text: Lessons 2 and 3 used the trend dimension, P(trend), to blend momentum and mean reversion. This lesson uses the volatility dimension instead, the same signal Chapters 3 and 4 built, to decide when option-selling strategies deserve weight and when option-buying strategies do.
Two Opposite Bets on Volatility Itself

body.caption: Options selling and options buying, side by side

A calm or range-bound regime, low realized volatility

children.text: The Volatility Risk Premium: Why Selling Usually Wins, Until It Doesn't

A well-documented empirical fact across equity index option markets globally, India included, is that implied volatility tends to run above the volatility that subsequently gets realized, on average. This is called the volatility risk premium, and it is the reason options selling wins more often than it loses in calm and normal conditions: sellers collect a persistent premium for bearing rare, tail-level risk. The same edge is exactly what makes short-volatility strategies dangerous, because it is only persistent on average, not in every single instance, and the rare instances it fails are the ones that matter most. The old trading floor description of this trade, picking up pennies in front of a steamroller, exists for a reason.

body.label: XIV, February 5, 2018
body.value: Lost more than 90% of its value in a single session
body.context: XIV, an exchange-traded note that profited from persistently low and falling implied volatility, was structurally exposed to exactly the volatility risk premium described above. A sudden, sharp VIX spike that day erased years of accumulated gains in hours, and the note was terminated shortly after. It remains one of the most cited real-world cautionary tales in volatility trading.

body.text: The volatility risk premium is real and persistent on average, but 'on average' includes the tail events that wipe out short-volatility positions. Never size a short-volatility strategy as though the premium is a guaranteed payment; it is compensation for bearing a risk that occasionally, and without much warning, actually materializes.

children.text: Regime-Conditioning the Selling vs Buying Mix

body.caption: The same linear blending logic from Lesson 2, now applied to the volatility regime probability from Chapter 3 or 4 instead of the trend regime probability

children.text: Notice this never fully switches off options selling, even in the Stressed row, and never fully switches off buying, even in the Calm row. A regime probability is an estimate, not a certainty, and a weighting scheme that respects that is more robust than one that makes an all-or-nothing bet on the model being right.
A Second Signal Worth Adding: The Premium Itself

The regime label alone is not the full picture. The actual gap between India VIX and recently realized volatility, the volatility risk premium in numbers, is an independent, useful check. If India VIX sits at 18% while 20-day realized volatility runs at 12%, that is a healthy 6-point premium supporting a selling bias, consistent with a calm regime. If India VIX sits at 22% while realized volatility has already climbed to 24%, the premium has inverted, realized volatility has caught up to and passed implied, and that is a warning sign to cut selling exposure regardless of what the regime label alone says, because the market may be repricing faster than the fitted model has caught up to.

body.text: Use the regime probability as the primary signal and the implied-minus-realized volatility gap as a secondary check. Agreement between the two is a stronger basis for sizing than either signal alone, and disagreement between them, a calm regime label alongside a compressed or inverted premium, is exactly the kind of situation where reducing size, not trusting either signal blindly, is the right call.

body.title: When the Regime Label and the Premium Disagree
body.scenario: Your fitted model reports the Nifty is in the Calm regime with P(stressed) = 0.08, which by this lesson's formula gives a 0.92 selling weight. At the same time, India VIX has risen to 21% while 20-day realized volatility has climbed to 23%, an inverted premium.
body.prompt: Should you trust the regime label's 0.92 selling weight as is, or adjust it? What does the disagreement between the two signals most likely indicate?
body.modelAnswer: The disagreement is a warning sign, not a coin flip to resolve in favor of one signal. A regime model fitted on historical data can lag a fast-moving shift in actual market conditions, exactly the detection lag problem previewed in Chapter 1 and formalized in Chapter 7, so a 'Calm' label alongside a rising, now-inverted premium is more likely evidence that conditions are changing faster than the model has caught up to than it is evidence the premium is a fluke. The prudent response is to reduce the selling weight meaningfully below what the regime label alone suggests, closer to a neutral stance, until either the regime read updates or the premium normalizes, rather than sizing a short-volatility position at 0.92 confidence based on a label that the market's own pricing appears to be contradicting in real time.

body.title: The Lesson From XIV
body.question: What is the most accurate takeaway from the XIV example in this lesson?
options: The volatility risk premium is not real and short-volatility strategies never work

The volatility risk premium is real and persistent on average, but a strategy that is structurally exposed to it without any regime-conditioning or risk limits can be wiped out by the rare events the premium exists to compensate for
Exchange-traded notes should never be used to express any volatility view
This event proves that options buying always outperforms options selling
body.explanation: XIV is a cautionary tale about unmanaged exposure to a real, persistent edge, not evidence that the edge itself is fake. The volatility risk premium genuinely exists on average; the lesson is that any strategy harvesting it needs regime-conditioning, position limits, and tail-risk awareness, exactly what this lesson's blended weighting and premium check are designed to provide.

points: Options selling profits when realized volatility undershoots implied; options buying profits when it overshoots, the volatility dimension's version of momentum versus mean reversion

The volatility risk premium, implied volatility running above subsequently realized volatility on average, is real and well-documented, and is why selling volatility tends to win more often than it loses in calm conditions
That same persistent edge is what makes unmanaged short-volatility exposure dangerous; XIV's near-total loss on 5 February 2018 is a widely cited real-world example of this risk materializing
The same linear blending logic from Lesson 2, now driven by P(stressed) instead of P(trend), sets a selling-versus-buying weight that never goes fully to zero on either side

The implied-minus-realized volatility gap is a useful secondary signal; disagreement between a calm regime label and an inverted premium is a warning to reduce size, not a tie to break in either direction
